content: `apply_one` calls `store::load_all(conn)` and runs two linear scans of every memory row on each invocation. When called inside `apply_from_consolidation`'s per-proposal loop this becomes O(M*N) full-table scans plus 2*M extra sweeps. Either hoist the `load_all` into a single `OnceCell<HashMap<...>>`/batch prelude in `apply_from_consolidation` and reuse it across proposals, or replace with targeted SQL lookups (`find_by_key_tag` for the key check and a `SELECT ... WHERE kind='lesson' AND content = ?` for the content check) so each proposal does at most one indexed probe.

When `embed_text` returns `None`, `apply_one` is invoked with `embedding=None`, which makes `store::insert_item`'s cosine similarity merge gate inert. In that path a near-duplicate of `p.suggestion.text` against an existing foreign-keyed memory is never detected, so `ConflictRefused` is impossible and the lesson silently overwrites nothing — but the audit/apply path still records `Applied` and writes the ledger. The current `evolution.embed_failed` warn is not enough: either skip such proposals (don't apply at all) or surface them as a distinct `EmbeddingUnavailable` outcome so they cannot bypass the anti-hijack check.

`super::change::read_all(&cr_path).unwrap_or_default()` silently swallows IO/parse failures into an empty `rows`, so `unique_change_id_for` derives `chg-<pid>` (or similar) without seeing existing entries. The local `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` only serializes within this process; another instance, the panel write path, or an external tool can still race. Result: collisions are only surfaced as an `append_change` error, and the apply has already counted the proposal as `Applied` in `report`. At minimum log the read failure and treat as a Warn audit, or hold the read-and-derive-inside-lock pattern with explicit error propagation.

TOCTOU race on the JSONL append path. `entry::read_all(&path)` is followed by per-iteration `entry::append(&path, &entry)` with no file locking, so two concurrent callers — e.g. `evolution::post_consolidation` racing with the "shadow 钩子" the doc comment explicitly says depends on this file — can both read the same baseline, both find no duplicate, and both append, silently breaking the dedup invariant that this whole function exists to enforce. Add a process-local `Mutex` (cheap, covers the same-process case the comment describes) or, better, an OS-level advisory lock (e.g. `fs2`/`fd-lock`) taken around the read–append window; failing that, re-read and dedup per-entry right before each append (still racy but at least narrows the window).

Partial-write semantics break the documented contract. If `entry::append` fails on the Nth proposal, entries 0..N-1 are already persisted on disk but the function returns `Err` with an incomplete `written` Vec (which is dropped at the `?`). The doc comment says "通知中心按此逐条落消息", so the caller (notification center) cannot tell which IDs were persisted: a naive retry can silently re-emit notifications for entries that already made it, and a naive rollback leaves the jsonl in a half-written state that may also trip the next call's `read_all`. Either build a tmp file in-memory and rename it onto `path` only after the whole batch succeeds (atomic-ish, also fixes the append-mid-line hazard), or document the partial-failure contract explicitly and return a typed error carrying the IDs that did get written.

evaluate_s2 unconditionally returns Allow and ignores the proposal (`_p`), so any proposal routed through this function — including irreversible ones — is approved. Safety relies entirely on an external caller-side filter that this function does not enforce or verify. Enforce the reversibility/impact invariant at the decision boundary itself (or at minimum, return a typed error/Result so callers must prove the pre-filter ran) rather than relying on a comment-documented invariant outside the API.

The loader honors externally configured `s2_active` even though evaluate_s2 is an allow-all placeholder. A misconfigured or tampered bot-config.json can flip the system into S2 and approve main-memory writes before any real policy exists. Either reject `s2_active` while the placeholder is in place, or require an explicit "policy_implemented" flag before honoring it.

This test explicitly asserts that high-impact proposals are approved by evaluate_s2. With the always-allow placeholder, any regression that removes the documented pre-filter would still pass. Add a test that exercises the irreversibility/impact guard at the actual decision boundary (or assert via a typed error/Result from evaluate_s2) so the safety invariant is enforced and verified, not just trusted.

Hard constraint ② (no sandbox bypass) depends entirely on the caller. `can_transition(Approved, Active)` unconditionally returns `true`, and `transition` does not consult any policy. The module doc itself flags this: "调用方忘记挂策略门 = skip-canary 硬约束失守". Every caller site that drives `Approved → Active` must independently consult a kill-switch / skip-canary config; this file provides no guard. Add an integration-level test (or a wrapper helper in this module) that asserts `transition(Approved, Active)` is rejected when the skip-canary flag is off, so the invariant cannot regress silently.
existing_code:
// Approved
        | (Approved, Canary)
        | (Approved, Active)         // skip-canary 配置
        | (Approved, Rejected)

content: `append()` opens with `OpenOptions::create(true).append(true)` but never calls `sync_all()` / `sync_data()` and performs no explicit inter-process locking. Two concurrent appenders (e.g. Tauri command handler and a background worker) can interleave bytes mid-line and produce unparseable jsonl; a crash between `write_all` and flush can leave a truncated final line that silently halves the last record on the next read. The "锁契约" comment defers to an external contract — there is no defensive check, fsync, or temp-file rename-to-append here, so a single missing lock at any call site silently corrupts the file. Consider `fs2`/`fd_lock` for advisory locking, or append-and-rename via a sibling temp file.

`ChangeStatus` is a bare 9-state enum with only `is_terminal()` / `as_str()`. There is no `can_transition_to(&self, next: ChangeStatus) -> bool` (or builder/setter enforcing one) — any caller can persist any state into any record. The 9-state machine contract (`Pending → Shadowing → ShadowPassed → Approved → Canary → Active`, with `Rejected` / `RolledBack` / `Expired` as terminals) lives only in doc comments. Nothing prevents e.g. `Active → Pending`, a backward jump after rollback, or `Expired → Active`. With a `Mutex<ChangeRecord>` + setter, or a simple `validate_transition` helper called at every write site, you can make these impossible states unrepresentable.

The "theoretically unreachable" fallback uses `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()`, which is **not guaranteed unique** within the same millisecond. Two concurrent callers (panel toggle / shadow / apply CR all route through this per the docstring) can both exhaust 2..=9999 in the same millisecond and produce the **identical** `chg-<pid>-<ms>` suffix — reintroducing the exact "二次回滚永久卡死" bug class this function exists to prevent. Use a process-local `AtomicU64` counter, a UUID suffix, or `rand` — anything monotonic or with collision-grade randomness.
existing_code:
// 理论不可达兜底：时间戳后缀保证唯一
    format!("{base}-{}", chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis())

content: The 14-day TTL is never enforced: this helper only stores a deadline, and the current production code does not read `expires_at_ms` to transition `Pooled` entries to `Expired` (or otherwise expire them). Consequently, every ordinary entry remains pooled indefinitely as well. Add an expiration predicate and invoke it on the production load/consume paths; computing the timestamp alone does not implement the documented TTL.

The production entry point `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app` is the only production caller, but every `#[tokio::test]` in this module exercises only `shadow_apply_for_batch` with `new_for_test`. The S0/S1/S2 routing (`S2Active → evaluate_s2 → Allow/Block`), the in-lock dedup against `ChangeStatus::Pending|Shadowing|ShadowPassed`, `unique_change_id_for` derivation, the `spawn_blocking` window holding `lock_evolution_store`, and the `evolution.not_reversible / evolution.blocked / evolution.shadow_dedup_hit` audit branches are all uncovered. Given this is documented as the only production path and carries the documented safety invariants (「本入口是生产唯一入口」), a dedicated e2e covering at least one happy-path S0 batch, one S2 Block batch, one S2 Allow batch, and one `is_reversible=false` proposal is required.

Global `TOTAL_WRITES` / `FAILED_WRITES` are `static AtomicU64` shared by both `shadow_apply_for_batch` and `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app`, never reset in production. The threshold check at the end of both functions uses `TOTAL_WRITES.load()` (cumulative ratio across all batches and across both call paths), so a single historical failure batch keeps the `evolution.shadow_warning` audit firing on every subsequent healthy batch (cumulative failed/total stays > 5% forever), and the very first batch can spuriously alert if the cumulative rate from earlier runs is already above threshold. The check should use per-batch counters (locally incremented, then compared against `FAILURE_THRESHOLD`) rather than the global atomics, or the atomics should be reset to zero on each batch's evaluation.

`shadow_apply_for_batch` is `pub async` but performs synchronous filesystem IO (`sink.write_change` → `change::append_change`, an `open + writeln` syscall) directly on the calling task without `spawn_blocking`. The doc comment correctly flags it as test-only, but `pub async` exposes it to any future caller on the Tauri async runtime, which would pin a tokio worker exactly the way `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app`'s comment warns against. Either downgrade it to a non-`async` synchronous `fn`, make it `pub(crate)`/`#[cfg(test)]`-gated, or wrap the write in `spawn_blocking` so the invariant holds regardless of caller.

Timestamp validation: reversed windows are only debug-asserted, so release builds silently report metrics for an end-before-start observation window. Additionally, `now_ms - window_start_ms` and `now_ms - app.applied_at_ms` are direct i64 subtractions on externally-sourced timestamps; corrupted JSONL values (or extreme system clock skew) can overflow in release (wrapping) or panic in debug, producing wildly misleading metrics. The public `compute` API takes raw timestamps and should validate/reject reversed windows explicitly (returning a `Result` or saturating with a documented error) rather than relying on `debug_assert!` and a `.max(1.0)` floor.

Sub-day window normalization: `.max(1.0)` forces any duration below one day to behave as a 1-day window, contradicting the documented formula `proposals_in_window / days_in_window`. A 1-hour window with 100 proposals reports ~100/day (correct: ~2400/day). Either drop the clamp (the division is already safe since the debug_assert guards the lower bound) or compute with millisecond precision and surface the actual fractional days; the current code systematically underreports candidate generation for sub-day observation windows.
existing_code: let window_days = ((now_ms - window_start_ms) as f64 / 86_400_000.0).max(1.0);

content: Rate cohort / denominator mismatch: only `candidate_generation_rate` is filtered to the observation window. `approval_rate` divides `promoted_count` (all proposals, ever) by `proposal_total` (all proposals, ever), and `rollback_rate` divides `rolled_back_count` (all ChangeRecords, ever) by `promoted_count` (proposals, ever). When a proposal owns multiple ChangeRecords, `rollback_rate` can exceed 1.0, and the lifetime vs. window semantics are undocumented. Pick one cohort (window-scoped or lifetime) and apply it consistently to all four metrics; if lifetime is intentional, rename fields and document it.

Survival join key identity: applications are indexed only by `mem_key` and the first occurrence wins. `AppliedRecord` also carries `proposal_id`, and `ChangeRecord` carries `proposal_id` and `change_id` — yet none are used. When a `mem_key` is reused across proposals or re-applied, every active change sharing that key is attributed the first applied timestamp, skewing the survival average. Either join on `(proposal_id, change_id)`/application-event identity, or enforce uniqueness of `mem_key` at write time; relying on `iter().find`-equivalent "first match" semantics hides a real data-integrity hazard.

The 5-item cap is a raw input-order truncation, which lets a leading run of Low-impact Distill or Medium-impact Merge proposals starve High-impact Contradiction proposals that the severity model is supposed to surface. Test `derive_caps_at_five` only checks length, not impact ordering. Either sort/filter by `impact` before truncating (High > Medium > Low) or document explicitly that order is FIFO and severity is not considered.

Proposal IDs are computed by joining arbitrary `String` ids with a literal `|` separator and no escaping, so two distinct sets can produce identical hash input. Example: `ids=["a|b","c"]` and `ids=["a","b|c"]` both sort to `["a","b|c"]` (different sort orders!) — `["a","b|c"]` joined with `|` is `"a|b|c"`, and `["a|b","c"]` joined is also `"a|b|c"`. The same hazard applies to Contradiction: `keep="a", drop="b|c"` collides with `keep="a|b", drop="c"`. This silently collapses distinct candidates under dedup. Fix by length-prefixing each ref or using a separator that cannot appear in id strings (e.g. `\u{1F}`).
Same delimiter-collision hazard on the Contradiction branch. Two keep/drop pairs that differ only by where a `|` falls inside an id produce identical hash input and collide in dedup.
existing_code:
let base_id = proposal_id(category, &target, &summary);
            let id = short_hash(&format!("{base_id}|{keep}|{drop_id}"));

content: Segment ③ walks `mark_human_applied` using the `cr.status` captured back in segment ①, then unconditionally writes `changes[pos] = cr.clone()`. If another caller mutates the same CR during segment ②'s apply window (e.g., `rollback_change_locked` flips status to `RolledBack`, or shadow/auto-apply advances it past Pending), segment ③ will silently overwrite that external status and resurrect a rolled-back CR. The re-`load_changes` here only re-locates by `change_id` — it never copies the file-side `status` back into `cr` before calling `mark_human_applied`. Fix: after re-loading, take `cr.status = changes[pos].status` (or skip the transition path entirely) so the write-back reflects the freshest persisted state.

`delete_by_ids` runs first; if it succeeds and then `rollback_applied` errors, the source mem_items are already gone but the apply-side lesson (key_tag `evo:<id>`) is left orphaned. The function returns the partial count and the caller (`delete_inner`) writes the proposal/CR as deleted, then propagates the error — so the user sees a failure but the lesson is permanently orphaned (still surfaced via injection_block, referring to a deleted proposal). Either run `rollback_applied` first (lesson first, refs second; on lesson failure nothing is changed), or commit both inside a single SQLite transaction so a mid-failure rolls both back.

Step ordering in `delete_inner` deletes the proposal line and pending CR rows before the optional cascade_source runs. If cascade_source fails (DB locked, disk full, SQLite busy), the function returns Err but the proposal and CRs are already gone — the next retry returns "proposal {id} 不存在" while orphan mem_items (source refs + lesson) remain in the DB, and the user has no visible way to retry the cleanup. Either reorder so cascade runs before the jsonl rewrites, or make the cascade failure a non-fatal warning (log + propagate only the proposal/CR deletion result) since the orphan mem_items are still recoverable from the proposal_id key_tag.

DB_WRITE_LOCK held across the entire snapshot read. The mutex is acquired before open_db() and only released when the function returns, so every other DB-using caller (read or write) is blocked for the full duration of open_db + ensure_table + load_all. Holding a synchronous lock across I/O is also a cancellation hazard — if the surrounding task is dropped mid-query the lock is held until the JoinHandle is dropped without running the guard's Drop. For a read-only snapshot, prefer a short-lived lock just around the I/O call, or split into open + (lock + read + unlock) so other writers are not stalled.

Silent mutex poison recovery hides corruption. `e.into_inner()` after a poisoned MutexGuard unpoisons the lock and lets the function proceed as if the lock were healthy. The original panic may have occurred in the middle of a write transaction — at that point the on-disk state (or in-memory invariants protected by the same lock) can be inconsistent, and this recovery masks that fact from every later caller. At minimum, this should return an Err("mutex_poisoned") instead of forging ahead and emitting only an eprintln line.

The proposal_id is inserted into the 24h dedup map and `EmitReport.written` is incremented BEFORE the AppHandle is checked and BEFORE `audit_event!` is invoked. As a result, a startup-order mistake (AppHandle not yet registered) or any audit-side failure silently drops the audit row while the proposal is permanently suppressed from re-emission for 24 hours. The public API exposes no audit outcome; `EmitReport.written` reflects "claimed by dedup" not "audited". Consider either (a) inserting the dedup record only after a successful audit, (b) extending `EmitReport` with a `not_audited`/`audit_failed` counter and returning a Result, or (c) at minimum reverting the dedup claim in a catch path so retries remain possible until the audit actually succeeds.

Lost-update race: this is a separate process-local mutex from APPLY_POLICY_WRITE_LOCK at line 63, yet both `set_apply_policy_at` and `set_derive_thresholds_at` RMW the same `bot-config.json`. If a caller (e.g., settings page) toggles the policy while another path writes thresholds, both threads can read the same baseline, each modify a different field, and the later `atomic_write` silently overwrites the other setter's changes — even though each individual replacement is atomic. Replace the two locks with a single shared mutex (or per-file lock) covering every writer to that file.
existing_code: static DERIVE_THRESHOLDS_WRITE_LOCK: std::sync::Mutex<()> = std::sync::Mutex::new(());

content: Fail-open governance on any read error: only JSON parse failure is logged; every other `std::io::Error` from `read_to_string` (PermissionDenied, IsADirectory, transient antivirus/backup lock, broken symlink, etc.) is silently mapped to `ApplyPolicy::Auto`. A user who has explicitly selected `confirm` can have their governance choice silently bypassed by a transient filesystem hiccup. Same pattern at lines 119-125 for derive thresholds. Consider distinguishing "config truly unset" (default Auto) from "config present but unreadable" (preserve last-known or fail-closed) and surface all read errors via `eprintln!` for diagnosability.

Semantic contradiction with the documented header comment. The header says `all_auto_apply` only disables *automatic* apply and manual/human approval is still allowed, but `should_shadow_only()` is OR-true under `all_auto_apply`, so any downstream apply path that gates on `should_shadow_only()` (rather than on `should_auto_apply()` alone) will silently block the explicitly approved manual write too. Verify the manual apply entry only consults `should_auto_apply()`, or split the predicates so shadow-only and auto-suppression can be distinguished.

Safety-critical configuration is permissive by default and accepts unknown fields. `#[serde(default)]` makes every missing field `false` (i.e. automation on, notifications on, shadow off) and unknown keys such as `all_auto_aply` are silently ignored, so an operator typo or partial `kill_switch: {}` block silently re-enables automatic apply. For a kill-switch, consider `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`, a typed constructor, or a validation step that fails closed on empty/typo'd input.

pub struct KillSwitch {
    #[serde(default)]
    pub all_auto_apply: bool,

content: `read_all` 与 `append` / `rewrite_jsonl` 之间没有任何同步。多个调用点（如 `panel::commands::load_proposals`、`precompute_human_apply_embedding`）在没有持 `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` 的情况下调用 `read_all`，若与 `append`/`rewrite_jsonl` 并发执行会读到正在写入的半行 JSON，`read_jsonl` 会把这种行当作损坏并把整文件备份为 `.corrupt`，导致正在追加的条目永久丢失。请在文档中明确该函数必须在 `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` 持有下调用，或把公开 API 改为内部并集中加锁。

`c.to_ascii_lowercase()` only handles ASCII A-Z; non-ASCII uppercase letters (e.g. `Ä`, `É`, `Ω`, Cyrillic `М`) are returned unchanged. This silently breaks the documented "uppercase → lowercase" contract for any non-ASCII input — the same problem described with different casing/diacritics will produce different `proposal_id`s, defeating the cross-language dedup goal. The inline comment about `is_numeric` correctly switches to Unicode semantics, but the lowercasing branch did not. Either use `c.to_lowercase().next().unwrap_or(c)` (Unicode full-mapping) or apply `char::to_lowercase` and accept the iterator, and extend the test suite with cases such as `"Ä"` vs `"ä"` and `"É"` vs `"é"` to lock the behavior.

`is_reversible` is a coarse 2-rule predicate that ignores the actual mutation surface of the proposal. It returns `true` for any non-`ToolSchemaHint`/non-`High` proposal even when `Suggestion.structured_patch` is `Some(_)` (Phase 1 invariant is documented but not enforced at the type level — see `Suggestion` and its public `Option<String>`), and even when the target is `SkillDsl` or `MemoryPolicy`, which can rewrite executable DSL or persistent policy. Since shadow/activation routing "depends on it" (per the doc comment), a `true` here can authorize an irreversible action. Either include `structured_patch.is_none()` and target-kind checks in the predicate, return the patch-presence as a separate signal, or restrict the reversible branch via a newtype/constructor that statically forbids patches.

The doc comments assert a strict data-minimization contract ("**不**存原始堆栈 / 文件路径 / 用户输入" / "**不**存原始路径 / 对话内容"), but the fields are plain public `String`/`Vec<String>` with no validation, no newtype wrapping, and no constructor. Anyone constructing an `EvolutionProposal` (including a future `Deserialize` consumer if audit input is ever re-ingested) can persist absolute file paths, stack traces, or PII into the audit stream, and the type system will not complain. Either (a) wrap these fields in newtypes (`TraceId`, `ToolName`, `MemoryId`, `SanitizedSummary`) so callers cannot accidentally construct invalid values, or (b) add a validating constructor used by the audit writer that rejects/redacts the disallowed content before it ever reaches the public struct.

TOCTOU race + overwrite violate the documented "不覆盖" invariant. `backup.exists()` returning false does not guarantee another concurrent reader hasn't just created it (or is about to); `std::fs::copy` always overwrites the destination, so whichever caller's copy runs second clobbers the original forensic snapshot. Additionally, the copy is non-atomic with concurrent appends — the snapshot can capture an arbitrarily torn intermediate state. Use a single atomic `create_new` (open with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` semantics, e.g. `OpenOptions::new().write(true).create_new(true)` + manual copy, or `fs::rename` after writing to a unique tempfile), or guard the whole "check + copy" sequence under the store lock that the file's writer holds.

Gate whitelist uses `matches!` patterns on enums that are NOT `#[non_exhaustive]` (verified in `proposal.rs` lines 44-51 and 86-92: both `ProposalCategory` and `ImpactLevel` are plain enums). Adding a new variant — e.g. `ImpactLevel::Critical` or `ProposalCategory::LoggingHint` — will compile cleanly and silently reject the new variant (the `matches!` returns `false`), contradicting the doc's explicit "未来新增 impact 变体必须显式 opt-in" design intent. The type system will not flag missed updates. Consider marking both enums `#[non_exhaustive]` (forces update sites to be revisited), or — at minimum — adding a `#[test]` that asserts the patterns stay allow-lists (e.g. lock the discriminant count) so silent expansion is caught in CI.

Wall-clock forward jumps (NTP slew, manual clock adjustment, VM clock drift) inflate `duration_ms` and falsely trip the `> 60s` sampling rule. `saturating_sub` only neutralises negative durations; a forward jump of even a few minutes will over-record traces and distort audit signal. Consider clamping `duration_ms` to a sane upper bound before sampling, or capturing `started_at_ms` and `ended_at_ms` from a monotonic clock (`std::time::Instant`) for the duration measurement while still emitting the wall-clock timestamps in the audit record.
existing_code: let duration_ms = ended_at_ms.saturating_sub(ctx.started_at_ms);

content: `emit_dedup_works_without_app_handle` asserts that `AppHandle` is unregistered, but `register_app_handle` is a public function with no test-only guard; if any other test (in this crate or an integration test) ever registers a Wry handle, this assertion silently flips to passing `written` as a real audit count instead of the intended eprintln path. `EMIT_TEST_LOCK` only serializes tests within this module, so concurrent callers in other modules invoking `emit_proposals` (e.g. via `post_consolidation` or directly) can perturb the count-delta checks (`before`, `before + 1`, `after_first > before`). To make these tests deterministic, either make the dedup map and `APP_HANDLE` injectable (so each test builds a fresh state) or expose a `#[cfg(test)]` reset hook that drains `EMITTED` and clears `APP_HANDLE`.

content: `validate_attach_path` (lines 409-428) canonicalizes the user-supplied path and inspects only the resolved extension — it does not verify that the canonical path lives under any allow-listed directory (e.g. user's home, app data dir, or a project root). The accompanying comment claims "用户在对话框亲手选的文件 = 明确授权", so the design trusts the caller; this assumption is fine for the chat-dialog picker, but the function is `fn` (no `pub`/`pub(crate)`) and is only invoked from `build_attachment_blocks`, whose input comes straight from the `attachments: Option<Vec<String>>` invoke parameter — which an attacker (or a malicious frontend module) can fabricate. The current behavior will happily open any readable .docx/.xlsx/.pptx/.pdf on the host (e.g. `/etc/shadow.docx`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pdf`, browser cookies exports). At minimum, add a directory-containment check (e.g. `canon.starts_with(allowed_root)`) or take the allowed-root list as an argument from the trusted caller.

Retry loop only retries JSON validation failures; provider/network errors break immediately, contradicting the module doc "失败重试 1 次" and the function comment "失败重试 1 次，再失败降级空 questions". A single transient API/5xx error therefore permanently skips clarification instead of honouring the promised one retry.

Only the attachment *count* is bounded (≤10); each path string is forwarded as-is to `build_attachment_blocks` and then into the prompt / error messages. A renderer/XSS can ship a multi-MB single path that (a) bloats memory and (b) gets injected verbatim into the model prompt and audit error text, providing a free exfiltration / cost-amplification vector. Reject paths that exceed a sane limit (e.g. OS PATH_MAX, 4 KiB) before any further processing.

Mutex poison recovery silently masks panics: `attempts.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` extracts the inner value from a poisoned mutex without re-raising or logging. If a task panics while holding this lock (e.g. mid-update of the attempt counter), subsequent operations silently use the torn state, potentially writing inconsistent attempt counts (rework loop at line ~749 has the same pattern). Prefer `.unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!("[workflow_runner] attempts mutex poisoned: {e:?}"); e.into_inner() })` or propagate the poison to the controller's error path.

Severity: high — affects audit accuracy and rework accounting.

Best-effort DB writes silently dropped, leaving engine state inconsistent with DB. `write_node_result` only broadcasts on `db_upsert.is_ok()`; on failure the new `node_result` (with `status`, `acceptanceVerdict`, `attempt`, `ms`) is lost. But the controller then computes `let ok = column_done && !fused && result.is_ok() && !acceptance_failed;` from the pre-write in-memory state and emits a `NodeOutcome{ ok, .. }`. So the engine may report `ok=true` while the DB still shows `status=success` for an acceptance-failed node (or vice versa). The same TOCTOU pattern appears in `mark_note_prefix` (skip/熔断 notes can be lost) and `reset_node_for_rework` (column reset to Todo can be lost, causing rework loop to skip a node that is still Done and refused by `run_task_in_chat`). Document the invariant or surface write failures to the controller.

Severity: high — produces wrong audit/rework behavior.

respond_core 的 notif_get 仅校验存在性、不检查当前 status。即便通知已被前一次应答置为 DONE、或被 invalidate_workflow_questions 置为 DISMISSED 后再次应答，仍会无条件 notif_resolve 并调用 brief_insert（卡级 + 全局级各一条）。这意味着：用户对同一问题双重点击 / 重试时会产生重复 brief 记录（一次应答多出 4 条 brief），与函数注释里「幂等 Ok(None)」的承诺不一致；亦会让「重跑生效」场景出现误写的担忧。建议把 notif_resolve 改为条件 UPDATE（`UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND status='pending'` 并检查受影响行数），受影响为 0 时直接 Ok(None)，并相应把 brief_insert 也包进同一个事务。

测试覆盖同样缺失：现有测试只对同一 qid 调用一次 respond_core，没有验证「重复应答」或「DISMISSED 之后应答」两条分支的幂等行为，建议补一个连答两次后断言 brief 计数为 1 的回归用例。
